entries.title: In Gary, Indiana, a month after historic NIPSCO power outage, families still wait for relief
entries.summary: <p>Inside Melissa Dixon’s home in Gary, the lights are back on. Her refrigerator is working. And she’s playing music as she does yard work. The generator that she had on her front steps is gone now. </p><p>It's more than a month since Dixon and hundreds of thousands of others in Gary and across northwest Indiana were left without power, some for at least <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/graphics/weather/powerless/12-nights-without-power-in-Gary-Indiana/" target="_blank" ><u>two weeks</u></a>, and she's still feeling anxious.</p><p>It wasn’t until recently that she finally did a big grocery haul. Until then, she'd been buying only enough food for a day or two.</p><p>“I don’t want to put food in here or buy food for a couple days,” Dixon says, “because I don’t want to lose my food again.”</p><p>She was among nearly 375,000 of the Northern Indiana Public Service Company's customers — of the 500,000 it serves — who were without electricity for days after an Aug. 11 derecho. </p><p>Gusts of 99 miles an hour were recorded at the Gary/Chicago International Airport. But Gary was one of the last communities to have power fully restored, U.S. Rep. Frank Mrvan, D-Indiana, whose congressional district includes Gary, said in a letter to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission asking for a federal <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/08/31/indianas-governor-demands-probe-of-power-utility-during-tour-of-storm-ravaged-gary" target="_blank" ><u>investigation</u></a> of NIPSCO’s response.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-0e0000" name="image-0e0000"></a> <picture The church organized food giveaways and opened to neighbors who were without power. Now, the Rev. Eric Boone, Tree of Life's senior pastor, says families in Gary are staying afloat, but things aren’t completely back to normal. Some people regained power only to find out their refrigerators no longer worked, he says.</p><p>“Even though lights came on, people’s bank accounts didn’t bounce back,” Boone says. “People’s food, refrigerators and freezers didn’t bounce back. Some people got mold. Some people’s houses are wrecked. Some people lost their cars.”</p><h3>Health worries</h3><p>Outside Dixon’s home, a large tree branch that had fallen on a neighbor’s property has been cut into smaller pieces. That's for firewood she plans to keep in case another storm knocks out the power again.</p><p>Inside, Dixon has stocked her refrigerator with staples like milk and eggs. She gets waffles to satisfy her four daughters, who range in age from 12 to 22 years old. Her younger daughters are all back in school. The house is mostly quiet with them in class. But steps from the kitchen, Dixon says she's worried about dark spots along the walls in her basement. Maybe those are mold. She keeps two humidifiers running in the basement, where she typically sleeps.</p><p>“We’re sick because of the mold,” Dixon says. “I started feeling really weird, like my vision … a lot of pain in my face and my neck area and going down my arm and my shoulder.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Melissa Dixon points to spots she worries are mold.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Dixon says she started to feel sick soon after the power was restored. She was taking medicine to try to treat inflammation that has led to facial nerve problems.</p><p>She'd like to move her family out of her home temporarily — until she’s able to get it checked for mold and any necessary remediation. </p><p>But first she needs some support. She applied for disaster relief through the Federal Emergency Management Agency, but her application is still pending.</p><p>The only financial help she has gotten is a $150 voucher from her township. Calling hotline after hotline has been like trying to win a contest rather than just get relief after a natural disaster.</p><p>“It’s like calling a radio station,” she says. “‘Ooh, am I going to win these tickets?’”</p><h3></h3><p>Dixon is among more than 33,000 people in Lake County, Indiana, who have applied for relief money from FEMA. The federal agency says $48.19 million has been allocated for Lake County but didn't say how many applications have been approved.</p><p>Gary officials distributed an additional $500,000 in disaster relief to about 1,200 households. In a city of about 67,000 people, that’s also only a fraction of the possible need.</p><p>Shanequa Cauley is among those in Gary who have struck out on getting help. She lost power for about nine days. It took much longer for her employer's power to be restored. That meant she lost out on about three weeks of pay.</p><p>Cauley says she borrowed from a friend to pay her rent on time. Some of the meals she and her 7-year-old daughter ate during the first weeks after the storm came from the City Life Center, which provided free hot meals to families in Gary. The center later gave out vouchers for $300 to use at a grocery store.</p><p>But those meals have since ended. Cauley is hopeful she can get her finances in better shape before the end of the month.</p><p>“I’m praying by next week everything should be good,” says Cauley, who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/25/nipsco-filed-application-for-customer-rate-increases-amid-storm-that-ravaged-northwest-indiana" target="_blank" ><u>owes NIPSCO</u></a> about $89. “The first thing I’m going to do is get my NIPSCO caught up.”</p><h3>‘Refuse to be knocked out’</h3><p>Britney Rice, community adaptation program manager for the American Red Cross in Indiana, says caseworkers have been trying to connect Gary residents with the resources they need. Twenty-eight people are still living in temporary shelter, according to Rice, who says the Red Cross also assisted others in getting vouchers to stay at a hotel for 30 days.</p><p>Some people haven’t been able to replace the food they lost during the outage. For others, the Red Cross is helping get them into a better situation than they were before the storms, which could include helping them find a better job, Rice says.</p><p>“When people have been impacted by disasters and the trauma that goes along with it, and they kind of kick into survival mode, sometimes all they can see is what’s in front of them,” Rice says. “And they make decisions that, if they could have seen something much bigger, then they would have made bigger decisions.”</p><p>Boone says his Tree of Life congregation has been scrambling to get relief information out. There still are people trying to figure out how to get by, he says. But Boone says he’s been heartened by how people in Gary have come together.</p><p>“We are strong," Boone says. "We are some that don’t give in or give up easily. We might get knocked down, but we refuse to be knocked out.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d40000" name="image-d40000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3ebe81d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6313x3543+0+334/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff0%2F4a%2Fc73f88564d73b521ba913da2056d%2Fgaryupdate-260920-07.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c138c50/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6313x3543+0+334/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff0%2F4a%2Fc73f88564d73b521ba913da2056d%2Fgaryupdate-260920-07.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9473b45/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6313x3543+0+334/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff0%2F4a%2Fc73f88564d73b521ba913da2056d%2Fgaryupdate-260920-07.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Melissa Dixon still got a NIPSCO bill for $374. She wants the utility company to take responsibility for what she and her neighbors have been through." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9473b45/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6313x3543+0+334/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff0%2F4a%2Fc73f88564d73b521ba913da2056d%2Fgaryupdate-260920-07.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/82e53dc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6313x3543+0+334/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff0%2F4a%2Fc73f88564d73b521ba913da2056d%2Fgaryupdate-260920-07.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9473b45/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6313x3543+0+334/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff0%2F4a%2Fc73f88564d73b521ba913da2056d%2Fgaryupdate-260920-07.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Melissa Dixon still got a NIPSCO bill for $374. She wants the utility company to take responsibility for what she and her neighbors have been through.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Dixon says she and her neighbors need more help, and she wants NIPSCO to take responsibility for what they’ve been through. Despite the disaster, she still got a NIPSCO bill for $374.</p><p>“It’s too much going on behind this power outage that we had to go through for two weeks,” she says. “It’s too much behind it. And the little that I’m going through, I could just imagine what other people are going through. I thought my home was safe. And now look: Me and my kids are truly sick.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/graphics/weather/powerless/12-nights-without-power-in-Gary-Indiana/" target="_blank" >12 nights without power in Gary</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/photography/2026/08/29/how-we-photographed-historic-power-outage-gary" >How we photographed a historic power outage in Gary</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bb0000" name="module-bb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h4><b>Resources for Gary residents: </b></h4><ul id="rte-8e577230-b2e0-11f1-b4e7-c913838dcc8d"><li>FEMA is accepting applications until Oct. 25, which can be filled out online at <a class="Link" href="https://www.disasterassistance.gov/" target="_blank" >www.disasterassistance.gov</a>. The federal agency provides funds to cover emergency needs, like medical equipment and food, and to make home repairs.</li><li>The Indiana State Disaster Relief Fund can help residents replace or repair essential furniture, appliances or pay for needed inspections. Residents can <a class="Link" href=" https://app.brightharbor.com/signup/indiana-sdrf-june-august-2026" target="_blank" >apply online</a>.</li><li>To get help in person applying for FEMA and the state’s relief fund, residents can visit United Steelworkers Local 1014, located at 1301 Texas St., Gary, Indiana, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. from Sept. 23 to Sept. 25th. Residents can also stop by from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Sept. 28 through Oct. 2. The site will be part of the state’s “One-Stop Shops” to get state and federal disaster relief assistance.</li><li>To talk to a caseworker at the Red Cross, residents can call 1 (800) 733-2767.</li></ul><br><h4><b>How to help Gary residents: </b></h4><ul id="rte-8e577231-b2e0-11f1-b4e7-c913838dcc8d"><li>Tree of Life Missionary Baptist Church welcomes volunteers who want to help with relief efforts or their food pantry. They are located at 2323 W. 11th Ave., Gary, Indiana.</li><li>People interested in becoming a disaster volunteer with the Red Cross can visit, <a class="Link" href="https://redcross.org/volunteers" target="_blank" >redcross.org/volunteers</a>.</li><li>Hope Alliance of Northwest Indiana continues to distribute cleaning supplies and pays for residents to do loads of laundry. Volunteers interested in helping can call, (219) 316-0099.</li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Why Trump's tariffs are illegal
entries.summary: <p>President Donald Trump is trying to "shift the exercise of core tariff authority from Congress to the Executive Branch," three former trade officials warn <a class="Link" href="https://libertyjusticecenter.org/wp-content/uploads/Amicus-Brief-Wolff-Maruyama-Hills.pdf" target="_blank" >in a brief they filed last week</a>. If that sounds familiar, it's because Trump has attempted something similar twice before, only to be rebuffed by the courts.</p><p>This time around, the brief notes, Trump is relying on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, claiming "a sweeping power to impose broad, economywide tariffs untethered from the statute Congress enacted." That assessment is especially noteworthy because the brief's authors, who are urging the Court of International Trade to reject Trump's power grab, were intimately involved in drafting and enforcing Section 301.</p><p>One of them is Alan Wm. Wolff, who directed the Treasury Department's Office of Multilateral Trade Negotiations and served as general counsel for what is now the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative during the Nixon and Ford administrations. Wolff played a leading role in drafting the trade act and wrote the original version of Section 301.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-650000" name="module-650000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Wolff is joined by Carla Hills, the U.S. trade representative under President George H.W. Bush, and Warren Maruyama, who was a U.S. trade representative lawyer during the Reagan administration and the office's general counsel during the George W. Bush administration. Both have extensive experience in implementing Section 301, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/19/2411" target="_blank" >authorizes the trade representative’s office to impose tariffs</a> in response to a foreign "act, policy, or practice" that is "unreasonable or discriminatory' and "burdens or restricts United States commerce."</p><p>Section 301 "was enacted to address specific unfair trade practices by individual U.S. trading partners," Wolff et al. note. But the Trump administration views the provision as a license to impose sweeping tariffs on trading partners that account for nearly all U.S. imports, <a class="Link" href="https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/2026/july/ustr-takes-action-forced-labor-section-301-investigations" target="_blank" >under the pretext </a>that they have failed to "impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor."</p><p>The upshot of these "often sham 'investigations,'" Wolff et al. note, is a tariff regime strikingly similar to the one Trump tried to impose last year under the <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/50/chapter-35" target="_blank" >International Emergency Economic Powers Act</a>, a 1977 law that does not mention import taxes and had never been used to impose them. In February, after the Supreme Court ruled that the emergency economic powers act does not authorize tariffs at all, Trump switched to Section 122 of the Trade Act, which the international trade court said he had improperly invoked.</p><p>"The Section 301 tariffs appear to be a thinly disguised pretext for reimposing the President's IEEPA tariffs under the guise of dealing with forced labor," Wolff et al. say. As they see it, "nothing in the statute authorizes [the] USTR" to "justify tariffs of unprecedented breadth" by aggregating "dozens of separate investigations" and setting "a novel standard that foreign countries have not in the judgment of the USTR met."</p><p>Contrary to the statute's requirements, the findings underlying that determination do not specify how each of the targets has fallen short or how their supposed failures burden U.S. commerce. Nor has U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer explained why the tariffs can be expected to ameliorate the problem he claims to be addressing.</p><p>The trade act "imposed clear substantive and procedural limits on each tariff authority" it delegated, the brief notes. "It is not at all credible that Congress simultaneously conferred, by implication, an unlimited tariff power through Section 301, administered by a cabinet official, without any indication in the statute or legislative history that it intended to do so."</p><p>By asserting "an effectively boundless Section 301 authority through the aggregation of numerous investigations," Wolff et al. say, Greer "exceeds the limits established by Congress and upsets the constitutional allocation of trade powers." </p><p>But what do they know?</p><p>A thing or two, suggests the Liberty Justice Center, which <a class="Link" href="https://libertyjusticecenter.org/wp-content/uploads/002-Burlap-and-Barrel-v.-Greer-Compl-2026-07-24.pdf" target="_blank" >filed one of the lawsuits challenging Trump’s tariffs</a>.</p><p>"The people who know Section 301 best," it says, "are telling the [international trade court] that the administration is using the statute in a way Congress never designed it to be used."</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fd0000" name="module-fd0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydykkkjy-l-h/" target="_blank" >Alma Campos</a></h5><p><b>Before the Blitz</b>: Little Village faced displacement and gentrification pressures long before Operation Midway Blitz. The neighborhood's proximity to downtown and rapidly gentrifying Pilsen has fueled concerns that development could push longtime residents and businesses out. Additionally, the COVID-19 pandemic <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydykkkjy-l-k/" target="_blank" >brought another period of upheaval</a>, forcing some businesses to close and leaving others struggling.</p><p><b>Midway mayhem</b>: During the height of Operation Midway Blitz, federal immigration agents detained 3,841 people, according to our analysis of federal data. Little Village became one of the most visible targets. Federal agents made arrests in the neighborhood on the first full day of the blitz and returned repeatedly in the months that followed. Fear of immigration agents kept people home. Shops and restaurants emptied, battering Little Village’s commercial corridors.</p><p><b>After effects</b>: Immigration enforcement is quieter and less visible now, but the Trump administration continues to arrest hundreds of people each month. In Little Village, many continue to stay home, and some business owners are spending money accumulated over generations to remain open. Some are questioning whether they can afford to stay.</p><p><b>In their words</b>: We spoke with residents, business owners and a neighborhood realtor about how immigration enforcement is reshaping Little Village — straining businesses, prompting property offers and leading some residents to invest in Mexico as they reconsider their futures in Chicago.</p><p><a class="Link" new album and homecoming show</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydykkkjy-l-tk/" target="_blank" >Selena Fragassi</a></h5><p>Without the Northbrook Public Library, Krewella may have never happened.</p><p>"It was an embassy of music for us and an incredible resource for records. We'd dive into the treasure chest of CDs and then rent them and upload them at home on iTunes," recalls Jahan Yousaf. Along with younger sister Yasmine, the duo first plotted out the electronic dance music project in 2007 while still enrolled at Glenbrook North High School. "Another huge influence for us was pirating music with Napster or LimeWire," Jahan added, laughing at the memories.</p><p>Old-school technology is a major theme on Krewella’s latest album "Peak," which abounds with messages about our collective obsession with the proverbial hottest new things and trying to find euphoria in an ever-changing world.</p><p>Grappling with the life twists and thinking about "how things used to be" takes on extra meaning for the now Los Angeles-based sisters as they return home to play Sound-Bar on Saturday.</p><p>"There was a party every single night when we [lived in Chicago]," Yasmine said. "Chicago is so deeply embedded in dance music, and I feel like it’s always going to be."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydykkkjy-l-tu/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>With the Bears' home opener set for Sunday, we want to know: What's your tip for a sports fan tailgating outside one of Chicago's stadiums for the first time?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). We may run your answer in a future newsletter or story.</i></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Michael Lansu</p>

entries.title: Vecinos de Bridgeport y Chinatown presionan a Amtrak para que frene plan para una yarda de ferrocarril
entries.summary: <p>Funcionarios de Amtrak y promotores inmobiliarios se enfrentaron el jueves a miembros de la comunidad, que se oponían a los planes de construir una enorme yarda ferroviaria en Chinatown, Bridgeport y Armour Square tan pronto como a finales de este año.</p><p>El plan, encabezado por la empresa Canal Edge LLC, de <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/06/justin-ishbia-white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-ownership-winnetka" target="_blank" >Justin Ishbia</a>, copropietario minoritario de los White Sox, incluye una propuesta para que los Sox jueguen en una instalación de uso mixto a lo largo del Río Chicago llamada The Railyards, en el South Loop, y para que la instalación de mantenimiento de Amtrak se traslade al vecindario en Canal Street, entre las calles 33rd y 35th.</p><p>Cientos de residentes, algunos vestidos con camisetas que decían “Protect our community, stop Amtrak’s rail yard” (Protege nuestra comunidad, alto a la yarda ferroviaria de Amtrak), llenaron la reunión. Las tensiones aumentaron cuando los líderes de Amtrak y los desarrolladores afirmaron que no habría impactos significativos sobre el medio ambiente ni la calidad de vida de los residentes cercanos al sitio propuesto.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-130000" name="module-130000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Los residentes respondieron cuestionando los estudios que Amtrak ha realizado sobre los impactos en la seguridad, el medio ambiente, el ruido y otros factores. El proyecto ha recibido $600 millones y una exclusión categórica del gobierno federal para evitar ciertas pruebas ambientales y una declaración de impacto ambiental con el fin de acelerar el inicio de las obras, pero los residentes también pusieron eso en duda.</p><p>“Nos están tratando como si fuéramos idiotas. No somos idiotas", dijo un residente. "Somos personas inteligentes y trabajadoras que hemos hecho de este lugar nuestro hogar".</p><p>Steven Segerlin, que dirige el desarrollo comercial en Amtrak, dijo que la empresa necesita un nuevo sito para un patio de mantenimiento que reemplace su instalación actual en calle 14th. El sitio renovado permitiría a la compañía modernizar sus prácticas de mantenimiento, limpieza y almacenamiento, lo que reduciría las demoras.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Cubs star Alex Bregman, teammates watch his horse Act of Parliament win at Churchill Downs
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman is hot at the plate, and his horse was hot at the track on Thursday.</p><p>Act of Parliament won his first race in four career starts, taking a $20,000 maiden claiming race by less than a length at Churchill Downs in front of Bregman and his teammates, who were enjoying a day off.</p><p>The Cubs made the roughly 100-mile trip from Cincinnati to watch the colt, who finished third by five lengths in his previous race Aug. 26 in Indianapolis. With Axel Concepcion aboard, Act of Parliament beat 10 others 3 years old and up and finished the 6 1/2 furlongs in 1:18.07. </p><p>Here's how Thoroughbred Daily News described the race: "A well-backed 3-1 second choice dipping down in class to take on $20,000 maidens, Act of Parliament was one of the last away after getting pinched back at the break, but looped his rivals on the turn and finished well to graduate by 3/4 of a length.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/ULxcg7Gstkw?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Alex Bregman wins race at Churchill Downs as Chicago Cubs teammates cheer him on"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>“It was electric,” trainer Will Walden told TDN. “To have Alex and the entire team here and then have the horse come through like that made it a pretty special night.”</p><p>According to Horse Racing Nation, Bregman Family Racing acquired Act of Parliament in August for $75,000, after he initially was purchased for $750,000 in 2025. But the race marked the end of Bregman's connection to the colt. Equibase reported that new owners claimed him for $20,000. </p><p>Still, Bregman won $27,108 of the $48,000 purse. Act of Parliament paid out $8.68 off a $2 bet to win.</p><p>Bregman has been in horse racing since 2022, according to Horse Racing Nation, winning 12 stakes races and earning more than $3.5 million in five seasons. </p><p>On the diamond, Bregman has been rolling since the All-Star break, batting .305 with a 1.007 OPS and 17 home runs in 56 games.</p>

entries.title: Hatred for data centers is sky high, but this local government agency sees dollar signs
entries.summary: <p>Polls show data centers are widely hated. Chicago and other cities are working to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/11/mayor-brandon-johnson-chicago-moratorium-data-centers-new-regulations" >slow the proliferation</a> of high-tech centers.</p><p>But the government body that oversees Cook County’s sewer system and manages stormwater sees data centers for artificial intelligence as an opportunity to pad its almost $2 billion, largely taxpayer-funded, annual budget.</p><p>The Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago, the owner of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/11/chicago-deep-tunnel-thornton-reservoir-flooding-calumet-south-suburbs-smell-mwrd-tarp-climate-change" >Deep Tunnel flood-control system</a>, stands to bring in millions of dollars in potential new revenue if it can sell treated sewer water to data centers and other industrial companies.</p><p>Data centers — being built at a rapid pace to support artificial intelligence applications — present a timely opportunity.</p><p>Americans are skeptical about AI’s benefits and are feeling a growing — largely bipartisan — dislike of data centers in particular. Almost 60% of people surveyed said they were concerned about the impact on water supply, while an even greater number voiced alarm about the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2026/05/13/comed-electric-customer-bills-rising-ai-data-centers-pjm-energy-costs" >effect on electricity prices</a>, according to a recent poll conducted by the University of Chicago.</p><p>The water reclamation district cleans the water that goes into our sewers, both rain and everything that is flushed down our toilets and sinks. That water gets sanitized and then placed back in Chicago-area rivers where it travels from local waterways all the way to the Mississippi River and eventually to the Gulf of Mexico.</p><p>While this sewer water is cleaned by the district, it’s not suitable for drinking. However, district officials have for years explored whether it could be sold to industrial users, many of which use fresh Lake Michigan water. So far, the district hasn’t struck any deals, but the board that oversees the agency passed a resolution last year to seek opportunities to sell water.</p><p>Data centers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/08/20/data-centers-ai-artificial-intelligence-chicago-illinois-great-lakes-michigan-drinking-water-jb-pritzker" >use an enormous amount of water</a> for cooling operations.</p><p>Earlier this year, district officials discussed a possibility of locating a data center next to one of its water treatment plants, according to internal emails reviewed by the Sun-Times.</p><p>In a statement, the district’s executive director John Murray said that no deals are in the works.</p><p>“There are no discussions with data center developers,” he said.</p><p>The district is open to serving the data centers, however. It owns thousands of acres of riverfront land that is leased to industrial companies. It also has explored the possibility of building pipes that would pump water directly to businesses.</p><p>“We see the potential for industrial reuse of our high-quality reclaimed water to protect our fresh drinking water supply and potentially generate additional revenue,” the district said in a separate statement.</p><p>It potentially eliminates the need for fresh Lake Michigan water to be used to cool the massive data centers, which can exceed 1 million square feet in size. Drinking water depletion is a major concern related to these high-tech facilities, which also use enormous amounts of energy. There are more than 200 data centers in the Chicago area.</p><p>The district held discussions earlier this year with a startup company known as MicroLink, which is trying to design more sustainable data centers, though officials say nothing came of the talks. After an industry website published a listing for a possible data center site located at the district’s Stickney water treatment plant, discussions ended. The plant has a Cicero address, though it straddles the town and the village of Stickney.</p><p>Cicero officials were so concerned that a data center was being placed next to the district’s water treatment plant that the town’s board passed a resolution to oppose the idea.</p><p>That same meeting, town officials passed another resolution <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/07/27/hawthorne-race-course-horse-track-buyer-data-center-developer-stickney-cicero-ai-artificial-intelligence" >opposing a potential data center</a> at the site of the former Hawthorne horse racing track. A published report identified a major data center developer as the new owner of the Hawthorne site.</p><p>Cameron Davis, one of nine elected commissioners on the board overseeing the district, said it makes sense to preserve Lake Michigan water while also seeking new revenue.</p><p>“Our treated wastewater is valuable,” Davis said in an interview.</p><p>“Recycled water could be a revenue stream to reduce the pressure on taxpayers” and it reduces the amount of Lake Michigan water used for industrial purposes, he added.</p>
entries.author: Brett Chase

entries.title: Cook County Crime Stoppers forced to 'slow down' operations if group can't secure funding by new year
entries.summary: <p>Paul Rutherford was first introduced to the Cook County Crime Stoppers when the violence prevention group helped solve the murder of his 23-year-old brother Joshua Rutherford in Cicero over two decades ago. </p><p>Now, having worked with the organization since and serving the last couple of years as chairman, Rutherford says the group is running out of money — and if they can’t get stable funding, Crime Stoppers' operations will need to "slow down" starting Jan. 1. </p><p>"Fighting crime is a 24-hour operation," Rutherford, 56, said. "I had two health scares ... I can't do this any longer as a volunteer." </p><p>Rutherford had two strokes in the spring and has been balancing his crime prevention efforts with a full-time law firm job. He says he has maxed out his credit cards paying off tip rewards. </p><p>He has also submitted multiple grants, including to the Cook County Judicial Advisory Council, in an effort to secure funding. </p><p>"When you see a flyer for a missing person or fatal hit-and-run with a reward up to $1,000, that money is coming out of my pocket," Rutherford said. "Consistent funding is the goal." </p><p>The group's financial troubles come at a time where demand for their help is at a high. </p><p>Rutherford noted that the Crime Stoppers assisted with<b> </b>roughly 95 cases in 2022 and have<b> </b>helped with over 160 cases so far this year.</p><p>"I will receive emails from detectives, I'm getting follow-up calls from families of victims, and it's just it's taking a toll," Rutherford said. "I've been put on notice already that I need to focus on my job because that's what I'm being paid for."</p><p> "If I can get funding, I can do this full-time and hire staff," Rutherford added.</p><p>Every Saturday, Rutherford and his staff of three retired detectives go out to crime scenes anywhere in Cook County to knock on doors and try to gather tips. </p><p>"We don't have bulletproof vests, we don't have guns showing, we're out there as disguised as possible because we don't want the community to be targeted for providing information," Rutherford said. "We went on one case a week to now we're doing four cases on a Saturday, and sometimes during the week as well, because we're so behind and backed up."</p><p>"The need for us to be out there is important because it generates tips, generates leads," Rutherford added. </p><p>Ald. Raymond Lopez (15th) emphasized the importance of the group, especially in his ward related to a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/20/3-kids-among-6-critically-hurt-in-suspicious-2-alarm-fire-at-west-englewood-home-sources" target="_blank" >West Englewood arson</a> and, more recently, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/11/woman-fatally-shot-while-driving-crashes-in-back-of-the-yards" target="_blank" >murder of an OEMC dispatcher</a>. </p><p>"The Cook County Crime Stoppers are an invaluable addition to law enforcement," Lopez said. "It is so crucial for law enforcement to have in order to build better cases, stronger cases that result in convictions."</p><p>Lopez stressed that it was imperative for city council to have conversations and hearings "to see where exactly our commitment lies to solving crimes in the city with our partners and Crime Stoppers."</p><p>"We have to do better. We have to make sure that we are putting our money where our mouth is," Lopez said. "Every community is impacted by the violence that we see, and it's imperative that we all focus on what we know are tried and true measures of engagement, connectivity and prosecution."</p><p>"Crime Stoppers is a resource we know works, and it would be a fool's errand not to continue using a partner and a tool that we know works, and a slap in the face to the innocent victims throughout the city of Chicago," Lopez added. "The message that it would send ... is that we are no longer concerned with solving crimes."</p><p>Rutherford noted that roughly 95% of Chicago cases make up the organization's workload, and the group has gotten over 5,000 calls to its tip hotline number from Jan. 1 to Aug. 31. </p><p>"That tells you that people know who we are. People want to talk, but they don't want to talk because of the area they live in," Rutherford said. </p><p>Losing Crime Stoppers would make detectives' jobs more difficult. </p><p>"Losing Crime Stoppers is like losing [gunshot detection tool] ShotSpotter," Rutherford said. "We are a tool for law enforcement to obtain that information that they need for that missing piece of that puzzle."</p><p>Rutherford finds fulfillment in knowing the group's work helps some families impacted by violence get closure when an arrest is made. </p><p>"It's a team approach when it comes to this, but the fact that a family took the time to call and to thank me and my team for what we've done, you know, that is satisfaction," Rutherford said. </p><p>Even with the group facing financial hardships, Rutherford's message to the communities he works with remained the same. </p><p>"When it comes to crime, if anyone has information on a homicide or any any crimes within Cook County, they can call our hotline number at 1-800-535-STOP." </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.cookcountycrimestoppers.org/get-involved" target="_blank" ><i>Donations are being accepted on the Cook County Crime Stoppers’ website.</i> </a><br></p>

entries.title: Forty year sentence for woman who pushed her 3-year-old nephew into Lake Michigan at Navy Pier
entries.summary: <p>A 40 year prison sentence was handed down to a woman who pleaded guilty Wednesday to killing her 3-year-old nephew after pushing him into Lake Michigan at Navy Pier in 2022. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/10/4/23387203/charges-upgraded-to-murder-for-aunt-accused-of-pushing-3-year-old-nephew-into-lake-michigan" target="_blank" ><u>Victoria Moreno</u></a>, 38, threw Josiah Brown into the water off Navy Pier in 2022. She watched as he sank below without attempting to rescue him. Divers found him about 30 minutes later.</p><p>On Wednesday Cook County Circuit Judge Thomas Byrne found Moreno guilty of murder but mentally ill and sentenced her to 40 years in the Illinois Department of Corrections, according to court records. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" She received treatment from two hospitals and had been on medication for seven years.</p>

entries.title: Chicago murals: DuSable's partner, Kitihawa, honored at Ravenswood school
entries.summary: <p>Chicago founder Jean Baptiste Point DuSable has gotten a lot more attention than his wife, Kitihawa, and the contributions she made to the growth of Chicago.</p><p>Two woman and a Ravenswood school are aiming to change that with a new mural featuring Kitihawa and DuSable on the front and side walls of the North Park Elementary School annex at 2017 W. Montrose Ave.</p><p>DuSable "could have never succeeded without collaboration of Kitihawa,” says artist Noelle Garcia, who is a member of the Klamath Tribes in Oregon and lives in Highland class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jim Vondruska/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Kitihawa, a member of the Chicago region’s Potawatomi tribe, “was definitely his business partner dealing with the trading posts,” says Monica Rickert-Bolter, who lives in West Ridge and partnered with Garcia on the piece. Rickert-Bolter also belongs to the Potawatomi tribe. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/reset-with-sasha-ann-simons/2025/03/12/get-to-know-chicagos-founding-mother-kitihawa" target="_blank" >Kitihawa helped DuSable</a> work with and navigate her community, she says. The two made a strong team.</p><p>But not much else is well known about Kitihawa. Meanwhile DuSable was a French-Haitian explorer who is often credited as Chicago’s first, non-native founder. Lake Shore Drive was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2021/6/25/22550370/jean-baptiste-point-dusable-lake-shore-drive-chicago-city-council-vote-compromise" >renamed to honor him in 2021</a>. So, the two artists found it appropriate to feature Kitihawa as the front person on their mural, which was unveiled on Sept. 9.</p><p>“As Native American women, we can understand and empathize with Kitihawa,” Garcia says.</p><p>The mural was made by hand with paint specially formulated to adhere to brick and allow it to breathe, which in turn protects the paint from sloughing off, Garcia says.</p><p>On the alley wall facing east, the mural features Kitihawa writing in a book and gazing north into the distance. DuSable is behind her, looking like he’s about to hike southeast. Lake Michigan stretches behind them with dragonflies, turtles, tall seagrass and other native flora and fauna surrounding them.</p><p>On the front wall of the annex, a beaver swims under a window while a river otter sits up in the bottom right corner. Braided grasses stretch across both walls, while blue, pink and brown irises frame the top corner of the annex doorway.</p><p>Kitihawa and DuSable were painted in an anime style, which might make young people relate to them more, the artists say.</p><p>The women also helped create a curriculum for the North Park students, who will use the mural to learn more about the indigenous people who lived in and around what is now Chicago. Students and teachers asked questions about why Kitihawa and DuSable were drawn in a certain way, a jumping off point for the two artists to discuss traditional Native American imagery. Students contributed their own versions of native plants and animals, some of which made it into the mural. </p><p>The women say they're happy with the result and hope it inspires generations of students. Next <a class="Link" href="https://www.turtleislandkj.com" target="_blank" >they are working on a graphic novel</a>, telling the story of Kitihawa and DuSable.</p><p>“I’m shocked at how powerful it was,” Garcia says of the mural. “You can feel positivity resonating from this building.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-fullBleed> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: 3rd beluga dies from shuttered Canadian aquatic park
entries.summary: <p>A beluga whale at a Spanish aquarium died Friday, bringing to three the total number of belugas that have died since being shipped out of Marineland Canada this summer — including two at Shedd Aquarium.</p><p>Jelly Bean died “suddenly and unexpectedly” Friday, Oceanografic Valencia said in a statement.<br>“In recent days, Jelly Bean had experienced feeding difficulties, prompting the veterinary team to intensify her monitoring,” the Oceanografic statement reads. “During this period, she showed signs of improvement and remained responsive to her caregivers, while continuing to receive around-the-clock monitoring.”</p><p>The Spanish aquarium said it was too soon to give a cause of death.</p><p>The aquarium’s other Marineland beluga, Cleopatra, and four dolphins that also came from the Canadian park are all doing well, according to the Spanish facility.</p><p>Jelly Bean was one of two belugas trucked and then flown out of the shuttered Marineland Canada aquatic park during the summer. Ten Marineland belugas arrived at Shedd.</p><p>Peekachu, a 23-year-old female, died at Shedd Aug. 25. Then, Rain, a 20-year-old female, died Sept. 2, also at Shedd. Both had been rescued from Marineland. A third Shedd beluga, 34-year-old Beethoven, part of the aquarium’s resident population, also died Sept. 2.</p><p>Shedd continues to investigate the cause of death of all three belugas.</p><p>Shedd is part of a consortium of four U.S. aquariums, as well as Oceanografic, that together agreed to take the belugas languishing in Marineland, located in Niagara Falls, Canada. Marineland had faced criticism for years that its animals were living in unsanitary conditions.</p><p>The park closed to the public in 2024, and Marineland officials, citing extreme financial difficulties, had threatened to euthanize the whales if permanent homes couldn’t be found.</p>

entries.title: Violet Grohl kicks off a Riot Fest 2026 that sees 5 a.m. lines for headliners Twenty One Pilots
entries.summary: <p>Riot Fest 2026 kicked off Friday in Chicago's Douglass Park with a big cross-generational mix, featuring flagship bands of elder Gen X and younger groups beloved by Gen Z fighting for prime time spots.</p><p>Even for the independent festival, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/05/28/tool-twenty-one-pilots-pierce-the-veil-alanis-morissette-morrissey-riot-fest-lineup" >this year’s lineup</a> offered an interesting assortment — which is saying something. This year, Riot Fest is the only place you’ll see <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/books/2026/03/10/patti-smith-memoir-bread-of-angels-jeff-tweedy-interview-chicago" >Patti Smith</a> and Insane Clown Posse in the same weekend. Friday's lineup featured punk legend Iggy Pop up against the night’s ultimate headliners, Twenty One Pilots. The latter’s Skeleton Clique fans were seen lining up as early as 5 a.m., many of them admittedly first-timers to the annual end-of-summer fest.</p><p>Organizers of Riot Fest prepared for this, with a <a class="Link" href="https://riotfest.org/first-timers-guide/" target="_blank" >“first-timers guide”</a> on its website, laying out the proverbial welcome mat for the newbies who were anticipated to entries.title: Trump says he is banning CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House
entries.summary: <p>President Donald Trump said Friday that he was banning CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House due to what he called unfavorable coverage, and threatened that more such media prohibitions could be coming — offering his administration’s latest test of constitutional First Amendment protections guaranteeing the freedom of the press.</p><p>Trump has long bristled at news coverage he maintains casts him in a negative light, and has a history of filing lawsuits against news organizations, while lashing out at individual reporters in person or over social media.</p><p>The move follows the president's decision, in February 2025, to keep Associated Press journalists out of the Oval Office, Air Force One and other events too small for a full press corps, in retaliation for the news outlet’s decision not to follow his lead in changing the Gulf of Mexico’s name.</p><p>The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing. Since returning to office, however, Trump has pursued other legal action against a variety of different outlets, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the BBC.</p><p>Trump seeking to block White House access for CNN is especially notably, however, as it could upend the traditional five-network television pool that travels with the president and tracks his every move — meant to provide independent coverage of his actions and interactions for the Americans who elected him and the world.</p><p>In the social media announcement, Trump did not provide details on how the ban would be implemented.</p><p>It came moments before Trump spoke to reporters in the Oval Office as part of a health care event. He later planned to take the press pool to his golf club in Virginia for a meeting and dinner sponsored by his Super PAC before spending the weekend at Camp David — one of the few places reporters don’t follow him.</p><p>The president wrote on his social media site that effective immediately, “I am banning” CNN, MSNOW and Politico “from the White House as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”</p><p>“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” Trump wrote. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”</p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Bears report: Vikings rule QB Kyler Murray out
entries.summary: <p>What happened Friday at Halas Hall:</p><h3><b>Murray out</b></h3><p>The Vikings ruled out quarterback Kyler Murray, who was concussed in the first quarter of Sunday's opener. </p><p>Carson Wentz will <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/09/17/bears-vikings-podcast-caleb-williams" target="_blank" >start</a> against the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>, while La Grange Park native J.J. McCarthy, who went 1-1 against the Bears last year, will serve as his backup. </p><p>Murray was hurt on an illegal Packers hit. Wentz went 12-for-19 for 133 yards and three touchdowns Sunday, rallying the Vikings for 29-straight points in a win. He last faced the Bears in 2022, throwing for only 99 yards.</p><p>Standout right tackle Brian O'Neill is questionable with a knee injury. Receiver Jauan Jennings, who's missed practices for personal reasons all week, was ruled out.</p><h3><b>Clean bill of health</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The Bears don't have a single player on the injury report for Sunday. The 10 players that either missed practice or were limited this week — including right tackle Darnell Wright — will be able to play. Tackle Ozzy Trapilo, who ruptured his patellar tendon in January, was a full participant in practice for the first time this season and has no injury designation. Still, it'd be surprising if he wasn't inactive Sunday.</p><h3>Suh here</h3><p>Ndamukong Suh, who used to torture the Bears as the Lions' star defensive tackle, visited Halas Hall as an analyst for Sky Sports.<br></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Agente de Aduanas culpable de usar su arma y placa para agredir sexualmente a mujeres en suburbios de Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Simplemente no importa si las víctimas de Luis Uribe eran trabajadoras sexuales.</p><p>Eso fue lo que un fiscal les dijo a los miembros del jurado esta semana cuando pidió un veredicto de culpabilidad contra el oficial de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (CBP) que usó su arma y su placa para cometer agresiones sexuales violentas.</p><p>Es posible que una trabajadora sexual sea violada, les recordó el fiscal federal adjunto Richard Rothblatt. Que la roben. “Las trabajadoras sexuales”, dijo, “pueden ser creíbles”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b50000" name="module-b50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El jurado estuvo de acuerdo el jueves, dándole la razón a cuatro mujeres por sobre un agente federal cuya defensa llamó a las víctimas "mentirosas" y "estafadoras". El panel concluyó que Uribe, de 45 años, agredió sexualmente a las mujeres en los suburbios de Chicago en 2022, y lo condenó por una serie de delitos que podrían enviarlo a prisión por el resto de su vida.</p><p>También rechazaron la versión de Uribe de que le había tendido una trampa una red de prostitución china porque él se negó a ayudarles a eludir la ley migratoria de Estados Unidos, explicación que Uribe dio desde el estrado de los testigos en medio de un testimonio en el que fue acusado de contar "un chiste sobre violación".</p><p>Uribe no mostró una reacción evidente cuando se leyó el veredicto el jueves. Mantuvo las manos entrelazadas delante de él mientras estaba sentado en una mesa en la sala de la corte. Pero cuando terminaron los procedimientos, le dijo a alguien que “se cuidara” de su familia mientras lo llevaban a una celda.</p><p>El jurado halló a Uribe culpable de 10 cargos de privación de derechos civiles bajo abuso de autoridad y de un cargo de exhibición de un arma de fuego durante un delito de violencia. Uribe está bajo custodia federal desde su arresto en diciembre y enfrenta una pena mínima obligatoria de siete años de prisión.</p><p>El juez de distrito Jorge Alonso fijó la audiencia de sentencia para el 21 de enero.</p><p>Michael Clancy, el abogado defensor de Uribe, salió de la Corte de Justicia Federal Dirksen sin hacer comentarios. Un portavoz de CBP dijo que, en general, sus empleados “desempeñan sus funciones con honor y distinción.”</p><p>“CBP está comprometida a garantizar que todos los empleados sean sujetos a los más altos estándares de integridad, profesionalismo y conducta personal”, dijo el portavoz.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Registros de la Corte de Distrito</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Un gran jurado acusó formalmente a Uribe en los días finales de la campaña de deportaciones de 2025, el Operativo Midway Blitz, pero su enjuiciamiento no estuvo vinculado a ese agresivo operativo. Más bien, la condena de Uribe representa una victoria notable para la oficina del fiscal federal de Chicago, que ha sido <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/07/10/jueza-determina-que-el-fiscal-federal-de-chicago-violo-su-orden-de-secreto-en-caso-de-tren-de-aragua" target="_blank" >acusado de mala conducta</a> en sus procesos contra manifestantes del Midway Blitz.</p><p>Para hallar a Uribe culpable más allá de una duda razonable, los jurados tuvieron que dar crédito al testimonio de inmigrantes chinos que hablaban poco inglés, que testificaron a través de un intérprete y fueron a veces inconsistentes y tenían aparentes vínculos con el comercio sexual.</p><p>Rothblatt y el fiscal federal adjunto Jonathan Shih instaron a los miembros del jurado a comparar el comportamiento de las mujeres con el de Uribe. Una víctima estalló en llanto varias veces en el estrado, incluso cuando los fiscales le pidieron identificar a Uribe en la sala de la corte.</p><p>Se quejó de que se había puesto mareada, que no podía ver y que ni siquiera podía caminar. Pero dio una respuesta clara cuando un fiscal le preguntó <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/10/customs-border-protection-luis-uribe-rape-schaumburg" target="_blank" >qué le había pasado</a> en un hotel Days Inn de Schaumburg en octubre de 2022.</p><p>“Me robó el dinero”, dijo. “Me violó”.</p><p>La mujer dijo que el ataque comenzó cuando un hombre irrumpió en su habitación del hotel después de tocar la puerta. El hombre mostró una placa, explicó, la puso sobre una mesa junto a un arma y exigió su dinero.</p><p>Luego, dijo, la obligó a hacer sexo oral, la arrastró hasta la cama y la violó.</p><p>“Tenía mucho miedo”, dijo. “Tenía un arma”.</p><p>Uribe subió al estrado más tarde y dijo que “nunca violé a nadie”. Admitió visitar prostitutas y aseguró que tuvo relaciones sexuales consensuadas con las mujeres. Luego, cuando un fiscal le preguntó si había usado el “tiempo de acondicionamiento físico” para salir del trabajo y tener el encuentro en el Days Inn, Uribe hizo un chiste.</p><p>“Aún así hice buen ejercicio,” dijo.</p><p>“¿Estás describiendo la violación... como un buen ejercicio?” preguntó Shih, incrédulo.</p><p>“No fue una violación, fue sexo consensuado,” contestó Uribe.</p><p>Shih luego calificó el comentario de Uribe como “un chiste sobre violación”. Clancy reconoció que fue “horrible” y “grosero”, pero le recordó al jurado que un juicio no es “un concurso de popularidad”.</p><p>“Puede que no sea alguien que les caiga bien”, dijo Clancy sobre su cliente. “Puede que no estén muy contentos de que sea un agente de las fuerzas del orden… [Pero] no han comprobado más allá de una duda razonable que robó o violó a alguien”.</p><p>Un testimonio crucial pudo haber venido de una quinta mujer que admitió que Uribe nunca la hirió, sin embargo. Dijo que conoció a Uribe por primera vez en un hotel Red Roof Inn de Naperville, donde él pagó $300 por tener sexo con ella y otra mujer. Más tarde, dijo, Uribe le dijo que era “policía de inmigración”.</p><p>Dijo que intercambiaron números de teléfono y continuaron su relación. Admitió que tuvo tres o cuatro encuentros adicionales con Uribe después de su primer encuentro, encuentros que nunca les había contado a las autoridades federales.</p><p>Clancy describió a la mujer como la “jefa en Chicago de una red de prostitución que [está dirigida] por otra jefa, ubicada en China”. La mujer negó ser una “jefa”, pero dijo que su propia jefa en China la envió a reunirse con Uribe.</p><p>La reunión ocurrió en un buffet de mariscos en Hoffman Estates en marzo de 2022. La mujer dijo a los miembros del jurado que su jefa quería que obtuviera una fotografía de Uribe que luego se circuló dentro de su comunidad.</p><p>También dijo que la enviaron con una oferta para Uribe: sexo gratis una vez a la semana “para no hacerle daño a nuestras chicas”.</p><p>Uribe dijo al jurado que la mujer constantemente le pedía ayuda con asuntos migratorios, incluso para ayudar a su jefa a entrar a Estados Unidos desde China. Cuando él no quiso ayudar, dijo Uribe, ella lo expuso. Clancy incluso calificó a Uribe como “la víctima perfecta.”</p><p>Pero Rothblatt dijo que fue Uribe quien encontró “a las víctimas más vulnerables” entre las mujeres inmigrantes, “algunas de las cuales operaban en las sombras”.</p><p>“[Uribe] subestimó a estas mujeres, y ellas testificaron ante ustedes”, dijo Rothblatt a los miembros del jurado. “Estas víctimas tienen derecho al debido proceso según la Constitución, igual que cualquier otra persona”.</p><p>Y, dijo Rothblatt, Uribe “debe ser responsabilizado por lo que hizo, igual que cualquier otra persona”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Bears' offense left much to be unpacked in 59-point explosion, starting with TE Colston Loveland
entries.summary: <p>The only <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> player to generate anywhere near as much hype as quarterback Caleb Williams this offseason was tight end Colston Loveland.</p><p>The consensus has been that he’ll be top-five at his position, the go-to man in the passing attack and a breakout star. Then he got just two targets in the season opener, both in the third quarter, and finished with no catches, no yards and — very importantly, to many — no fantasy points.</p><p>Sound the alarm! Push the panic button! Demand a trade!</p><p>“Yeah, yeah, that’s what everyone thinks,” he told the Sun-Times as he laughed about the reaction to his stat-less game. “No, not a big deal at all. Whatever the role, as long as we get a win, that’s the only thing that matters.”</p><p>All the zeroes next to Loveland’s name in the box score are less cause for concern and more an indication of just how much coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/11/as-engineer-and-artist-blend-styles-bears-ben-johnson-gets-goosebumps-about-future-with-caleb-williams" >Ben Johnson</a> can still unpack as the season rolls on, continuing Sunday at home against the Vikings.</p><p>The Bears are coming off a blowout win over the Panthers in which they piled up 59 points, the fourth-highest in franchise history, including the playoffs and did so without utilizing some components of the offense that likely will be prominent over the course of a full season.</p><p>Loveland tops that list, though he was proud nonetheless of playing 87% of the snaps in the scorching heat — more than any other skill player — and when he looked at the Bears’ 7.5 yards per carry in the ground game, “I’d like to say I was a little part of it.”</p><p>On running back D’Andre Swift’s goal-line touchdown run late in the third quarter, Loveland helped clear a path by putting Panthers linebacker Jaelan Phillips on his back.</p><p>The upside is that Loveland was open on both of Williams’ throws to him, and a little better execution on both their parts would’ve led to connections. It won’t take much to fix it.</p><p>Loveland critiqued his own “route detail,” so he might not have been exactly where Williams expected, and Williams’ throws were off-target. He brushed those aside as “just a little miscommunication” and was confident they’d cash in on those opportunities against the Vikings.</p><p>Loveland ran unattended across the middle for what could’ve been a huge gain with plenty of open space ahead of him, but Williams threw well behind him. Later in the drive, from the Panthers’ 11-yard line, Loveland had a step on cornerback Mike Jackson in the end zone, but Williams threw too far ahead of him.</p><p>“There were a number of other times where he was the primary [receiver] and the ball just didn’t find him,” offensive coordinator Press Taylor said. “The great thing about Colston is that’s not a guy you worry about at all.</p><p>“When you’ve gone through three quarters and you have no touches and you continue to fight and continue to help others get in the end zone — You wouldn’t have known if he had 10 catches or zero catches at the end of the game in the locker room.”</p><p>Williams also threw for Loveland at the goal line in the fourth quarter, but that pass was tipped and intercepted by defensive lineman Bobby Brown, and the play was negated entirely by the Panthers’ Derrick Brown getting flagged for offsides.</p><p>No matter. Williams hit wide receiver Jahdae Walker for a touchdown two plays later.</p><p>The Bears pretty much scored at will without Loveland contributing as a pass catcher and kept several other weapons mostly on the shelf:</p><p>- Wide receiver Luther Burden had only five targets, catching five passes for 63 yards.</p><p>- Rookie speedster Zavion Thomas didn’t play a snap on offense.</p><p>- Swift got one pass, a 10-yard catch.</p><p>- The Bears ran only 12 plays in 13 personnel, which are formations with three tight ends.</p><p>“You’re still talking about last week, aren’t you?” Johnson said Friday with his signature irritated smile.</p><p>Only a little.</p><p>And only in the context of what could be coming next.</p><p>“You just don’t know where the ball’s going to go,” Johnson said. “We certainly look to involve all of them, especially when they’re as selfless as they are. They care about nothing more but to win... The selflessness, I commend them for that because it’s not everywhere.”</p><p>If it stays that way, it just adds to Johnson’s unpredictability as a play designer and caller. Imagine the work the Panthers put in on Loveland only for him to be used mainly as a bulldozer. The roster and the offense itself are built to give defenses too much to keep track of, and Johnson has plenty more to unveil.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Caleb Williams might be NFL's fastest QB — how will the Bears exploit it?
entries.summary: <p>With the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> tied late in the second quarter, Caleb Williams dropped back, stepped up into the pocket and ran up the left sideline.</p><p>Without a linebacker there to spy him, the quarterback took off at a full gallop at the Panthers’ 36. Defensive backs stayed plastered on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/09/17/bears-vikings-podcast-caleb-williams" target="_blank" >Bears</a> receivers, thinking Williams was still looking to pass.</p><p>“From there,” Williams, “it was just, 'Beat them to the pylon.’”</p><p>By the time Williams reached the end zone for a 29-yard touchdown run, not a single defender had touched him.</p><p>He hit 20.8 mph, the fastest any NFL quarterback ran in Week 1. Only four other ball-carriers ran faster.</p><p>How coach Ben Johnson wants to use Williams’ speed will dictate whether the Bears’ high-flying offense can continue playing at the next level. At the least, it’s given Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores something else to think about before Sunday’s home opener at Soldier Field. Williams, meanwhile, has another avenue at providing an encore to the best offensive performance of his pro career.</p><p>With Williams running 10 times for 65 yards last week, mostly on scrambles, the Bears scored 59 points, the fourth-most in team history. Williams became just the second Bears quarterback since 2003 not named Justin Fields to run 10 times in a game. He was the only quarterback in franchise history to run for at least 65 yards and two touchdowns — and also throw for at least 250.</p><p>“He’s always been a really, really high-level runner,” Johnson said Friday.</p><p>He has the best top-end speed of any quarterback in the NFL. Last year, Williams had five carries of more than 20 mph — as much as all the other quarterbacks combined. Only the Broncos’ Bo Nix had more than one. In Week 1, Williams surpassed 20 mph twice. Only the Jets’ Geno Smith did it once.</p><p>“He looked explosive, man,” receiver Luther Burden said.</p><p>Williams’ ability to throw the ball decisively and on time will be his biggest test all season long — but his speed will be the X-factor.</p><p>“That’s why he's so hard to prepare for,” Johnson said. “You know, these quarterbacks this day and age, they're able to use their legs just as well as their arms. I think it adds another dimension.</p><p>“It’s really challenging when you're on the defensive side looking to contain. You talk all week about keeping him in the pocket, forcing him to play quarterback. And yet that's easier said than done a lot of times, particularly when you've got a guy like him who is so good at escaping.”</p><p>When Johnson decided to take the Bears’ job, he was intrigued by not only Williams’ throwing ability but his athleticism. Lions quarterback Jared Goff averaged 1.6 yards per carry in the three years Johnson called plays.</p><p>Williams, who has averaged 5.2 yards per carry under Johnson, might be the answer to the question so many Bears fans asked earlier this decade — what would happen if you combined Fields’ rushing ability with a competent passer?</p><p>The Bears called designed runs for Fields, but don’t figure to often with Williams. As the play-caller, Johnson needs to strike the right balance between calling runs for his dangerous quarterback and exposing him to unnecessary hits.</p><p>Johnson is enough of a perfectionist that he wants Williams’ first read to be open, every time. But he appreciates what the quarterback can do — whether it’s running or scrambling — when it’s not</p><p>“If I had my druthers, every single play the primary receiver would get the ball in rhythm and timing,” Johnson said with a smile. “And yet there's plenty of times I don't call the plays against the right coverages or it didn't work out quite like we thought and [Williams} makes us right. . It's a luxury, for sure.”</p><p>Williams is all for it. He lost 15 pounds this offseason — he worked with a nutritionist and cut out sports drinks — in part to get faster.</p><p>“I know I sound like I'm old when I'm young, but when you start packing on a little weight it gets a little rough,” he said. “I feel good, I feel slim, I feel smooth in my movement. And I want to keep that up throughout this part.”</p><p>Seven of Williams’ 10 runs in Week 1 were scrambles. Another was a failed fourth-down quarterback sneak. The most clever, though, was when Williams faked a handoff and rolled right on a sweep with three blockers in front of him. When he tried to plunge into the end zone, he was hammered by Panthers safety Nick Scott.</p><p>That’s the kind of risk the Bears don’t want to take often.</p><p>“There's times where you got to lower your head and get a yard for us, whatever it may be, and I think he understands those,” offensive coordinator Press Taylor said. “I think there's always going to be a fine line you're balancing with your quarterback carrying the football, but it's something we feel like we can utilize in the right pieces. It gives us an advantage.” <br></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: 'Prime' Colorado vs. Northwestern spectacle should have been at new Ryan Field
entries.summary: <p>Out in Boulder, Colorado, this week, a world-famous football coach sat under a black ball cap, the gray hood of his “I AIN’T HARD 2 FIND” sweatshirt pulled over the top, dark shades hiding his eyes, a Coke-can-size gold cross hanging from the thick gold chain snaking around his neck, and paid compliments to one of his least-talked-about peers in the Power Four ranks.</p><p>“I really respect and admire him,” Colorado’s Deion Sanders, Pro Football Hall of Famer, said about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >Northwestern</a>’s David Braun.</p><p>Let’s just get this out of the way: <b>Colorado (+3½) at Northwestern </b>(6:30 p.m., Fox 32, 720-AM) would have been a great way to open the new Ryan Field, an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/02/03/northwestern-new-ryan-field-delay" target="_blank" >$875 million stadium project that fell behind schedule</a> enough that the first game won’t come until Penn State visits Oct. 2. Not that the Penn State game won’t be a huge deal; it will. But having “Prime Time” Sanders on hand to hype the new place would’ve been oh, so perfect.</p><p>Instead, it will be Northwestern’s final game at Martin Stadium on the Evanston lakefront. Expected thunderstorms could be a major factor in how things play out for the 2-0 Buffaloes and the 1-0 Wildcats, not to mention how it looks at the pop-up venue on national TV at night.</p><p>It also will be the first game for Braun — 20-19 since taking over for the fired Pat Fitzgerald — after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/09/17/northwestern-football-david-braun-contract-extension-big-ten" target="_blank" >Northwestern extended the former Big Ten coach of the year’s contract</a> for three years through the 2031 season. Whether or not Braun actually lasts that long will have a lot to do with his teams’ fortunes in a North Shore palace whose price tag screams for winning big in a college football world that’s more cutthroat than ever.</p><p>The Wildcats have had an extra week to prepare for their visitors, who have a hardfought win at Georgia Tech under their belts and a quarterback, Julian “JuJu” Lewis — a former five-star recruit offered by every top program in the country — upon whom Sanders’ vision relies even more than it did on signal-calling son Shedeur.</p><p>Over the last few seasons, opponents have knocked the Buffaloes around up front. Shedeur Sanders — now a Cleveland Brown — ran for his life, sacked 94 times in two years at Colorado. Winning at the line of scrimmage is going to be the key to victory for the Wildcats, but are they really at an advantage? Sanders rebuilt his lines — especially on offense — in the transfer portal and seems full of belief that his big’uns can go belly-to-belly with others’ big’uns.</p><p>“I like this task for us, I really do,” he said. “I don’t want to comment on [being] underdogs or none of that, because I’m not a betting man and I don’t think the kids give a darn about that and I’m not going to use that to propel them. If I’ve got to use that to propel them, something’s wrong with us. Let’s go.”</p><p>If the Wildcats can pressure Lewis all night and run the ball effectively on offense, they’ll be more than fine. I can’t help but wonder, though, where the ceiling might be with Sanders’ team. How high is it? Is Lewis a show-stealer? Is Colorado’s run game even better than people realize?</p><p>I’m taking the Buffs, 23-20.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure (AP Photo/Erin Hooley) ORG XMIT: ILEH113</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Erin Hooley/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p><b>OTHER WEEK 3 PICKS</b></p><p><i>All games are Saturday.</i></p><p><b>Southern Illinois (+39½) at Illinois </b>(1 p.m., Peacock, 890-AM): The Salukis will try to pound the rock against a defensive front Illini coach Bret Bielema admits is too small. It won’t show up dramatically on the scoreboard, but it’ll add up to just enough to cover a cartoonish spread. Illini, 52-14.</p><p><b>Florida State (+18½) at No. 10 Alabama </b>(2:30 p.m., ABC 7): Seminoles coach Mike Norvell is under such duress, he spent part of his week answering questions about a box truck — it sure looked like a moving truck — spied outside his home. This, the same week athletic director Michael Alford was canned by the school. Uh-oh. Roll Tide, 42-10.</p><p><b>Michigan State (+29½) at No. 3 Notre Dame </b>(6:30 p.m., NBC 5, 780-AM): In Hollywood, Fitzgerald would pull off a mega-upset and be carried off the field. He’s back! Sparty on! Look out, world! This ain’t Hollywood. Irish, 38-0.</p><p><b>No. 7 LSU (-2½) at No. 8 Ole Miss </b>(6:30 p.m., ABC 7): The hate toward LSU coach Lane Kiffin, formerly of the Rebels, is beyond extreme. Nobody slashes and burns like Kiffin, the most polarizing coach in college football. The Rebs are amped up to the max, but guess what? The Kiffster has the better team. Tigers, 27-23.</p><p><b>Northern Illinois (+33½) at Arizona </b>(9:30 p.m., TNT): Do we really need to watch this? The Huskies are so far in over their heads in this one, it’s rough stuff. Arizona, 45-3.</p><p>My favorite favorite: <b>No. 23 Louisville (-1½) vs. No. 16 SMU </b>(2:30 p.m., ESPN2): QB Lincoln Kienholz couldn’t crack the starting lineup in three seasons at Ohio State, but he’s crushing it through two games as Louisville’s lead dog. If you watched the Cardinals lose 41-38 to Ole Miss on a neutral field, you know how explosive they are.</p><p>My favorite underdog: <b>North Carolina (+3½) at Clemson </b>(11 a.m., ESPN): UNC’s Bill Belichick might be enveloped in scandal, but his defense is balling out. Tar Heels get the upset.</p><p><b>Last week: </b>4-3 straight-up, 3-4 against the spread.</p><p><b>Season to date: </b>10-4 straight-up, 6-8 against the spread.</p>

entries.title: It's never too early for Bears to make statement in bruising, relentless NFC North
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> finally made good on general manager Ryan Poles’ mission to “take the North” last season with their first NFC North title since 2018, but they were far from dominant in the division.</p><p>The first step toward becoming a true championship contender is establishing themselves as the bully of the North. That starts with handling the Vikings, whom the Bears face Sunday in their home opener.</p><p>A little over a year ago, the Vikings spoiled coach Ben Johnson’s debut with a fourth-quarter rally, and the Bears followed by getting crushed in Detroit the next week. They were the only of the NFL’s eight division winners to finish with a losing record in the division at 2-4.</p><p>Both of those wins, by the way, were late escapes in which the Bears were losing in the final 30 seconds. They needed a long kick return to set up their walk-off field goal against the Vikings in Minneapolis in Week 11 and an onside kick recovery to force overtime at home against the Packers, when they won on quarterback Caleb Williams’ 46-yard touchdown pass to DJ Moore.</p><p>Other divisions are more top-heavy than the North, such as the NFC West and its three contenders in the defending champion Seahawks, Rams and 49ers, but it’s the strongest from top to bottom.</p><p>The Packers and Lions have been consistently in the mix for the last few seasons, and while the Vikings have been up and down, they’ve never been a pushover under coach Kevin O’Connell.</p><p>It’s easy to forget that even amid their quarterback issues last season as former first-round pick J.J. McCarthy struggled, they still finished 9-8. They held their own by sweeping the Lions and split with the Packers and Bears.</p><p>Then, in a resounding message to anyone who had written them off this season, they hammered the Packers with 29 consecutive points at the end to beat them 39-22 last week.</p><p>The Vikings’ defensive strengths are well documented, and the chess match between Johnson and defensive coordinator Brian Flores is central to the game Sunday. Flores is an artist when it comes to blitzing and disguising, and he gave Williams and the Bears two vastly different looks last season.</p><p>But their offense is a concern, too, and that’s because O’Connell and the host of skill talent they’ve put in place. Anyone could step in and throw to four-time Pro Bowl wide receiver Justin Jefferson.</p><p>The Vikings will start journeyman Carson Wentz, on his sixth team in 11 seasons, because Kyler Murray is out with a concussion. Neither of them is particularly fearsome in a vacuum, but O’Connell has gotten by with less.</p><p>If anyone can bring out the best of them, it’s O’Connell. It also might be the Bears’ defense, which allowed an otherwise floundering Bryce Young to put up one of the best games of his career last week.</p><p>A reasonable goal for the Bears in the NFC North this season is to go 4-2, which would mean they need to sweep at least one of their rivals. It’s also going to be hard to do that if they can’t defend Soldier Field. So while it’s only Week 2 and it’s “only” the Vikings, this is an optimal time for the Bears to make a statement in the division.</p>
